entities.summary:
Juan de Borja Lanzol (Llançol) de Romaní, el mayor was the first of ten cardinal-nephews elevated by Pope Alexander VI, the cousin of his father, Galcerán de Borja y Moncada, in a scandalous power play that reshaped the papacy and European politics.

 Born in 1467 in Valencia, Spain, to a family of Catalan nobility, Romaní's rise to power was facilitated by his father's influence and his own charisma. He was known for his lavish lifestyle and his ability to secure lucrative positions for his family members.

Romaní's appointment as cardinal-nephew was a masterstroke by Alexander VI, who used his position to consolidate power and enrich his family. However, Romaní's time in the papacy was marked by controversy and scandal, including allegations of corruption and nepotism.

Despite his tumultuous tenure, Romaní's legacy as a key figure in the history of the papacy and European politics remains. He played a significant role in shaping the course of the Renaissance and the Protestant Reformation, and his family's influence can still be seen in the modern-day Catholic Church.

 'The papacy is a game of thrones, and Alexander VI is the greatest player of all time,' Romaní once said.
